Clap
klăp
v. (to strike the hands together; in Scripture both a shout of homage and a gesture of scorn)
Old English clappan, to beat or throb. The Hebrew taqa is to strike or drive, used of clapping hands and of blowing a trumpet — a percussive act.

Biblical Definition

The same gesture means opposite things in Scripture, and the difference is the object. Homage: “O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph” (Psa 47:1), a psalm that goes on to say why — “For the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth” (Psa 47:2). Creation joins in: “Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together” (Psa 98:8), and again, “all the trees of the field shall clap their hands” (Isa 55:12). Scorn: “Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place” (Job 27:23), and over the ruined city, “All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?” (Lam 2:15). The hands are the same; the heart behind them is not. Applause in Scripture is never neutral — it is either the acclamation of a King or the derision of the fallen.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to clap as to strike with a quick motion, to bring two things together suddenly with noise; and specifically, to applaud by striking the hands together.

expand to see more

CLAP, v.t. To strike with a quick motion, so as to make a noise by the collision; to strike with something broad, or having a flat surface.

2. To thrust; to drive together; to shut hastily; as, to clap a door.

3. To applaud; to manifest approbation by striking the hands together.

O clap your hands, all ye people. Ps. xlvii.

Key Scripture

Psa 47:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah. O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph."

Isa 55:12 — "For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands."

Lam 2:15 — "All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?"

Job 27:23 — "Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place."

Modern Corruption

Applause in the assembly is defended by Psalm 47 and attacked by nothing at all, when the question Scripture actually asks is who is being acclaimed.

expand to see more

Psalm 47 does command clapping, and it is honest to say so; the objection that any bodily expression in worship is fleshly cannot be sustained from a Bible in which hands are lifted, knees are bowed and the floods are told to clap. But the psalm attaches the gesture to a definite object and a stated reason. Clap your hands, all ye people — and then, for the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth. It is homage rendered to a King at His ascension, the same acclamation a returning conqueror received at the gate. That is a different thing from applause given to performers at the front of a room, and the difference is not fussiness. Where a congregation applauds a singer, a speaker or itself, the form of Psalm 47 has been kept and its object exchanged; and the regulative principle exists precisely to ask, of every element in worship, what God has appointed and to whom it is directed.

Lamentations supplies the other clapping and it should be read whenever the first is quoted. Men clap at ruined Jerusalem, hiss, and wag the head, and repeat her old titles back at her as a taunt — Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty? Applause of that kind is alive and well in every generation, and Christians are not immune to enjoying it when a fallen minister or a rival congregation supplies the occasion. Job's friend describes the same scene as the fate of the wicked, and the book's ending makes clear how badly a man may misapply that description to his suffering neighbour. Isaiah 55 is the promise that ends the matter: the day comes when the trees of the field clap their hands, and the thorn is replaced by the fir tree, for a name unto the LORD that shall not be cut off.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew taqa (H8628), to strike or clap; machaa (H4222), to clap or smite the hands, of floods and trees; saphaq (H5606), to clap in derision.

expand to see more

Hebrew taqa (H8628) — to strike, to clap, to blow a trumpet; O clap your hands, all ye people; Psalm 47:1.

Hebrew machaa (H4222) — to strike the hands together; let the floods clap their hands; Psalm 98:8, Isaiah 55:12.

Hebrew saphaq (H5606) — to clap, often in mockery or grief; men shall clap their hands at him; Job 27:23.

Hebrew sharaq (H8319) — to hiss, to whistle; the companion gesture of derision; Lamentations 2:15.

Hebrew teruah (H8643) — a shout, a blast; the voice of triumph in the same verse as the clapping; Psalm 47:1.

Usage

"“O clap your hands, all ye people” — homage to an ascending King."

"“All the trees of the field shall clap their hands” — creation at the restoration."

"“All that pass by clap their hands at thee” — the same gesture, turned to scorn."
